title: Plato

cards.b:
Plato (c. 427–347 BCE) was a student of Socrates and the teacher of Aristotle. Whitehead once said that the European philosophical tradition is "a series of footnotes to Plato".

UPSC asks about Plato's justice, his philosopher-king, his communism and his view of women. All four come from one book, the Republic.

He wrote after Athens lost the Peloponnesian War and after democratic Athens executed Socrates in 399 BCE. That shock shaped everything he wrote: he wanted a state run by knowledge, not by the crowd.

cards.h: Justice as doing your own job
cards.b:
For Plato, justice is not a law or a contract. It is harmony. Each part does the work it is best suited for and does not meddle in the work of others.

This works at two levels. In the soul, reason should rule, spirit should support it, and appetite should obey. In the state, the same order should hold between three classes.

So the just state is the soul "writ large". Plato studies the state because justice is easier to see on a big canvas.

cards.h: Three parts of the soul, three classes
cards.b: Each class has its own virtue. Rulers need wisdom, auxiliaries (soldiers) need courage, and producers need moderation. In fact, all three classes need moderation. Justice is the fourth virtue: the harmony of the whole.

Plato says the state's troubles will not end until philosophers become kings, or kings become philosophers.

Why philosophers? Because only they know the Form of the Good, the true standard behind all good things. Everyone else lives in the cave of opinion.

The allegory of the cave

Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows on a wall and think they are real. The philosopher escapes, sees the sun, and must return to rule, even though the others may mock him.

Rule, then, is a matter of knowledge, like steering a ship. You would not choose a ship's pilot by vote.

Plato's state depends on a long, state-run education: music and gymnastics for the young, then mathematics. The few who pass study dialectic from about thirty and begin to rule from about fifty.

To keep people content with their class, he proposes the myth of the metals, often called the "noble lie". Citizens are told that the god mixed gold into rulers, silver into auxiliaries, and iron and bronze into producers.

Movement is possible: a gifted child of producers can rise, and a weak child of rulers can fall. So it is a class system based on merit, not birth.

For the two guardian classes only, Plato abolishes private property and the private family. Guardians live in common barracks, eat together and own nothing.

Mates are arranged by the state, and children are raised in common, so no one knows their own parents.

His aim is not equality or economics. It is to remove the two great sources of corruption, greed and family loyalty, so that rulers care only about the common good.

Producers keep their property and families. So this is very different from Marx's communism, which is about the whole of society and about ending class rule.

In Book V, Plato argues that women can be guardians and even philosopher-rulers. The difference between the sexes, he says, is like the difference between bald and long-haired men: it does not matter for the job.

Some call this the first feminist argument. Others disagree. Julia Annas argued that Plato's aim was the state's efficiency, not women's rights. He also still says women are on average weaker.

Either way, it was radical for a city where women could not vote or own much property.

cards.h: From the Republic to the Laws
cards.b:
The Statesman

Plato ranks constitutions by whether they follow law. When there is no philosopher-king, rule under law is the second best.

The Laws

His last work. He drops the philosopher-king and proposes a mixed constitution that blends monarchy and democracy, with the rule of law at its heart. Private property returns, with limits.

So Plato moves from the ideal state to the second-best state. This shift is a favourite exam point.

• Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), called Plato's state totalitarian: rule by an elite, censorship of poets, and lies told to the people.
  • Aristotle said Plato's state seeks too much unity. Common property will be neglected, because what belongs to all is cared for by none.
  • Defenders such as Ernest Barker say Plato wanted rule for the people's good, not tyranny.
  • Democrats object that knowledge experts can be wrong too, and no one checks them.

In Book VIII of the Republic, Plato ranks five constitutions from best to worst. Each one decays into the next:

  • Aristocracy, the rule of the wise. This is his ideal.
  • Timocracy, the rule of the honour-loving, like Sparta.
  • Oligarchy, the rule of the rich.
  • Democracy, the rule of the many.
  • Tyranny, the rule of one man for himself.

Democracy, he says, is charming and full of variety. But it treats equals and unequals alike. Each person does as they please, and there is no order.

Too much freedom leads to its opposite. The people pick a champion to protect them from the rich, and that champion becomes a tyrant.

Plato's image is the ship of state. The sailors fight over the wheel and flatter the owner, who is strong but half-deaf. They ignore the true navigator, who studies the stars.

Scholars often compare Plato's three classes to the varna order: Brahmin, Kshatriya and the producing classes. But Plato's classes are based on talent, while varna became fixed by birth.

His idea of rule by experts echoes in debates on the civil services and technocracy, and in the case for an independent judiciary and Election Commission.

Gandhi admired Socrates and translated Plato's Apology into Gujarati in 1908.

"Plato's theory of justice is a theory of functional specialisation." Comment.
"Examine Plato's communism. How is it different from Marx's?"
"Is Plato an enemy of the open society?"

Structure: define justice at both levels, draw the three-class diagram, explain the philosopher-king and communism as tools of justice, give Aristotle's and Popper's critiques, then note the move to the rule of law in the Laws.

quiz.q: For Plato, justice in the state means…
o: Equal shares of property for all
Each class doing its own work without meddling
Obedience to the law made by the majority
Rule by those who own the most land
quiz.w: Plato's justice is harmony: each class does the job it is best suited for.

quiz.q: Plato's communism of property applied to…
quiz.w: Only rulers and auxiliaries gave up property and family. Producers kept both.

quiz.q: Which work has Plato propose a mixed constitution under the rule of law?
quiz.w: In the Laws, his last work, Plato settles for a second-best state under law.

quiz.q: Who called Plato an enemy of the open society?
quiz.w: Karl Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945).

quiz.q: The virtue Plato assigns to the auxiliaries is…
quiz.w: Rulers have wisdom, auxiliaries courage, and moderation is shared by all.

quiz.q: In Republic Book VIII, the constitution that decays directly into tyranny is…
quiz.w: Plato says excessive freedom in democracy leads to tyranny.

quiz.q: Plato's 'myth of the metals' says rulers have which metal in their souls?
quiz.w: Gold for rulers, silver for auxiliaries, iron and bronze for producers.

quiz.q: The allegory of the cave mainly illustrates…
o: The difference between opinion and true knowledge
quiz.w: Prisoners mistake shadows for reality; the philosopher sees the truth.

quiz.q: Who argued that Plato wanted women as guardians for the state's efficiency, not for women's rights?
Timocracy, in Plato's scheme, is rule by…
quiz.w: Timocracy is driven by honour, like Sparta.
